PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 71 — Lesson 95: Chronic Kidney Disease Management

FNP-level goal: Recognize chronic kidney disease as a longitudinal risk state, not a creatinine label. Confirm chronicity, classify filtration and albuminuria risk, protect kidney and cardiovascular health, steward medications, detect complications, and know when acute deterioration, electrolyte risk, or disease complexity requires urgent or nephrology care.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish CKD from acute kidney injury and understand why repeated eGFR and albuminuria data matter.
  • Use eGFR, urine albumin, trajectory, etiology, and comorbidity to estimate risk and monitoring needs.
  • Assess BP, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, medication exposure, volume status, and social barriers that affect kidney outcomes.
  • Recognize anemia, potassium, acid-base, mineral-bone, volume, and medication-safety complications of CKD.
  • Identify urgent deterioration, atypical findings, advanced disease, and referral patterns that need nephrology or emergency escalation.

Part 1 — CKD Requires Chronicity and Context

Chronic kidney disease is defined by persistent abnormalities of kidney structure or function with health implications. A single low eGFR or one elevated creatinine does not establish chronic disease; it may reflect acute illness, dehydration, medication effect, obstruction, laboratory variation, or muscle mass. Conversely, a seemingly acceptable creatinine can mask clinically meaningful reduction in filtration for a patient with low muscle mass. Interpret eGFR, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio when indicated, urinalysis, trend, and clinical context together.

The FNP’s first task is to ask: Is this chronic, acute, or acute-on-chronic? Review prior labs, symptoms, fluid loss, medications, blood pressure, urinary obstruction symptoms, infection, contrast or nephrotoxin exposure, heart failure, and recent hospitalization. Acute kidney injury is a safety problem; do not delay evaluation simply because the patient also has a chronic CKD diagnosis.

Part 2 — The Two-Axis Risk Model: eGFR and Albuminuria

eGFR estimates filtration. Albuminuria reflects glomerular injury and is independently associated with kidney and cardiovascular risk. Together, their persistent categories help estimate progression risk and guide monitoring, medication selection, and referral. Protein in the urine is not merely a laboratory nuisance; it may be a signal of diabetic kidney disease, glomerular disease, hypertension-related injury, or another process requiring a focused differential.

Trend matters more than one value. A stable eGFR over years differs from a rapid decline. A rising albuminuria pattern may change the risk conversation even if filtration appears relatively preserved. Confirm abnormal findings appropriately, review collection issues and urinary infection or menstruation when relevant, and avoid assuming every protein signal is due to diabetes.

Part 3 — Identify the Cause and the Modifiable Drivers

Common causes include diabetes, hypertension, vascular disease, glomerular disease, inherited disease, structural or obstructive disease, recurrent AKI, and medications. History should include diabetes duration and control, BP pattern, family kidney history, hematuria, stones, recurrent urinary infections, urinary retention symptoms, edema, rashes, joint or systemic symptoms, hearing changes, exposures, and medication use. Examine BP, volume, edema, skin and joint findings when clinically relevant, and signs of cardiovascular disease or obstruction.

Kidney protection is cardiovascular protection. Optimize BP, glycemia, smoking cessation, lipid and heart-failure care, physical activity within ability, vaccinations as appropriate, and avoidance of preventable AKI. The exact target or drug choice must follow current guidance and patient context. Kidney care is not a separate silo from diabetes, hypertension, and heart failure care.

Part 4 — Medication Stewardship Is Core Kidney Care

Review every prescribed, over-the-counter, herbal, and supplement product. Renally cleared medicines may need dose adjustment; insulin and some glucose-lowering agents may carry more hypoglycemia risk as eGFR falls; NSAIDs and other nephrotoxic exposures can be especially harmful in volume depletion, heart failure, or combined medication settings. Ask about nonprescription analgesics, proton-pump inhibitors, decongestants, supplements, and imaging or procedural plans.

Renin-angiotensin system medicines, SGLT2 inhibitors, diuretics, and other therapies may have important kidney, cardiac, or electrolyte benefits in selected patients but require context-specific monitoring. A modest laboratory change is not automatically treatment failure, and an abnormal value should not be ignored. Evaluate timing, volume status, BP, potassium, acute illness, indication, and trajectory; then use current protocols and consultation when needed. Avoid generic advice to stop all chronic medicines during every illness.

Part 5 — Monitor Complications Before They Become Emergencies

CKD may produce hypertension, volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia, mineral and bone abnormalities, pruritus, malnutrition, neuropathic symptoms, and uremic manifestations in advanced disease. The monitoring plan depends on stage, trend, albuminuria, cause, medication exposure, and patient stability. Teach patients which symptoms matter: reduced urine output with illness, worsening edema, dyspnea, palpitations, weakness, severe nausea, confusion, black stools, or signs of infection.

Hyperkalemia can disrupt cardiac conduction. Significant weakness, palpitations, syncope, ECG concern, or severe elevation requires urgent assessment. Worsening dyspnea, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, hypotension, confusion, severe metabolic symptoms, or concern for uremia also changes the setting from routine follow-up to urgent or emergency care.

Part 6 — Nutrition and Social Context

Nutrition counseling should be individualized to CKD stage, potassium and phosphorus issues, diabetes, heart failure, cultural food patterns, food security, and patient burden. Oversimplified lists can cause malnutrition, confusion, or avoidance of healthy foods. Engage kidney dietitian support when available and appropriate. Ask whether the patient can obtain medications, monitoring, transport, blood-pressure equipment, and recommended foods.

Health literacy and caregiver support are safety factors. Explain eGFR and albuminuria in plain language: how well the filter is working, whether protein is leaking, and why repeat tests matter. Teach the patient to bring all medications, monitor BP when indicated, report intercurrent illness, and know which symptoms require same-day or emergency care.

Part 7 — When to Refer

Nephrology referral is appropriate for advanced CKD, rapid or sustained decline in eGFR, rising albuminuria, uncertain etiology, active urinary sediment or hematuria concern, difficult hypertension, significant electrolyte or acid-base disturbance, anemia or mineral-bone complexity, inherited disease concern, and planning for kidney replacement therapy. Earlier referral can improve preparation, education, and avoidance of crisis dialysis.

Referral should have a clear question and a closed loop: What abnormality or decision needs support? What testing has already been done? Can the patient attend? Who reviews the consultation plan? The FNP continues to manage primary-care needs, vaccines, medication reconciliation, diabetes and BP care, and social barriers while specialist care proceeds.

Part 8 — Clinical Case: Acute on Chronic

A 70-year-old with stable CKD develops vomiting and diarrhea, continues an NSAID for back pain, and now has dizziness, decreased urine output, and a rising creatinine. FNP reasoning: this may be acute kidney injury on CKD. Assess volume status, BP, medications, potassium, systemic illness, and obstruction or infection concern; arrange the appropriate urgency of evaluation. Do not simply wait for the next routine renal panel.

Part 9 — Clinical Case: Albuminuria Is a Risk Signal

A 54-year-old with diabetes has preserved eGFR but repeated elevated urine albumin results and uncontrolled BP. The FNP explains that filtration is only one axis of kidney health. Confirm persistence, assess diabetes and BP management, review medication options and monitoring under current guidance, evaluate other urinary findings, and coordinate kidney-risk reduction rather than reassuring the patient that creatinine is normal.

Part 10 — Clinical Case: Potassium and Safety

A patient with advanced CKD reports weakness and palpitations after a recent medication change. FNP reasoning: assess immediate stability and obtain urgent evaluation for possible hyperkalemia or arrhythmia according to the presentation. Potassium abnormalities are electrical risks, not values to manage only through a delayed portal exchange.

FNP High-Yield Framework: KIDNEY

  1. K — Know chronicity: compare prior eGFR, albuminuria, symptoms, and acute exposures.
  2. I — Identify cause and trajectory: diabetes, BP, vascular, glomerular, obstructive, inherited, and medication clues.
  3. D — Determine risk: eGFR plus albuminuria, progression rate, cardiovascular disease, and complications.
  4. N — Navigate medicines: dose, nephrotoxins, interactions, volume, potassium, indication, and monitoring.
  5. E — Examine complications: BP, volume, anemia, potassium, acid-base, mineral-bone, nutrition, and uremic symptoms.
  6. Y — Yield to escalation: AKI, severe electrolyte or volume problem, rapid decline, atypical urinary findings, advanced CKD, or referral need.

Take-Home Summary

CKD is a chronic cardiovascular and metabolic risk state measured by filtration, albuminuria, cause, and trajectory. The FNP protects patients by recognizing acute change, optimizing modifiable drivers, practicing medication stewardship, monitoring complications, and referring early when complexity rises. Never manage creatinine in isolation; manage the patient’s kidneys, heart, medicines, risks, and ability to follow the plan.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace current CKD guidelines, renal-dose references, nephrology consultation, dialysis planning, or individualized emergency assessment. Oliguria with illness, hyperkalemia symptoms, severe dyspnea or edema, confusion, hypotension, or rapidly worsening renal function requires timely evaluation.
